Refactor the trigger-fire branch out of runOnePollCycle into a function that takes a signer + deepCoinId + deepPerTrigger + tpslVaultPackageId; call it from main() with the ephemeral keypair as signer. Tests can pass `signer: undefined` to skip submission OR (better) pass a fake signer to assert the build/submit path is exercised.

descriptions: discoverVaultsTick builds the JSON-RPC params as [query, { descending: false, limit: 50 }, cursor]. The actual suix_queryEvents JSON-RPC contract (and the SDK 2.x client confirmed at @mysten/sui/dist/jsonRpc/client.mjs:413-419) is positional: [query, cursor, limit, descending: bool]. The keeper passes the options object in the cursor slot, the cursor (when present) in the limit slot, and never passes the descending boolean. On the live sandbox this either errors out (params type mismatch) or returns an arbitrary subset of events depending on RPC tolerance, and the cursor is never honored — so AC3.8's 'discovers vaults' end-to-end path does not work against a real node, even though the unit tests pass (the network-shape test mocks the response and ignores params shape).

discoverVaultsTick calls parseVaultCreatedEvent and registry.addOrUpdate with the raw event-derived KnownVault (vaultRegistry.ts:97-106). That record has baseCoinType / quoteCoinType undefined (they are `?:` optional and the parser never sets them). The trigger loop in runOnePollCycle skips every vault that lacks these fields: `for (const vault of registry.iterate()) { if (!vault.baseCoinType || !vault.quoteCoinType) continue; }`. Result: the keeper discovers vaults, polls Pyth, but NEVER fires a trigger because the type tags needed for the execute_trigger<Base, Quote> call were never resolved from manifest.pools. The contract's 'Implementation guidance > Generic type arguments' explicitly required the keeper to resolve these from manifest.pools[]; the deliverable does not.

Even if R1-002 were fixed and the for-loop reached the fire branch, runOnePollCycle's only action is `logTriggerAttempt(...)` followed by a comment 'Note: trigger submission requires a signer, which is only available in the full boot path. In runOnePollCycle (test seam), we skip submission.' The main() boot path (lines 293-344) calls `runOnePollCycle` directly — it does NOT pass a signer and does NOT have a separate trigger-submit step. So even in the production path, `signAndSubmitTrigger` and `buildTriggerTransaction` are never invoked. Combined with R1-002, no `trigger_fired` line will ever be emitted. The triggerSubmitter module exists but is dead code.

The Sui suix_queryEvents JSON-RPC signature is [query, cursor, limit, descending_order]. The keeper builds params as [{ MoveModule: ... }, { descending: false, limit: 50 }, cursor?]. The second element is shaped like SDK options rather than the raw cursor argument the JSON-RPC method expects, and cursor (when present) is appended in third position. This is a coupling/abstraction confusion between the high-level SDK call shape and the low-level JSON-RPC raw-fetch shape. The networkShape.test.ts mock returns canned data regardless of params shape, so the bug never surfaces in tests.

Production must build, sign, submit, and call logTriggerFired/logTriggerFailed, then call registry.markTriggered.

The trigger loop iterates vaults, calls this resolver, then reads only the two oracles for that pool and applies the formula with the correct quoteDecimals.
Drop pollIntervalMs from PollCycleArgs entirely. Pass deepCoinId only when (and if) the same function is generalized to also submit triggers; otherwise also drop it from the read-only path.

Extract the production main loop body into a runMainTick(args, signer, signAndSubmit) function and have the network-shape test exercise it with a no-op signer. The function-under-test for T-009 should be the same code path production runs.

Add an inFlight: Set<string> on VaultRegistry. Before submission, registry.beginFire(vaultId) — returns false if already in-flight. After submission completes (success or failure), registry.endFire(vaultId). markTriggered is set on success only.
descriptions: runOnePollCycle is documented as the T-009 test seam and explicitly skips trigger submission with the comment 'In runOnePollCycle (test seam), we skip submission'. The production main() loop then calls the same runOnePollCycle for every tick with no separate signing/submitting path. As a result, the keeper's main loop logs trigger_attempt but NEVER calls signAndSubmitTrigger, never invokes the Ed25519 keypair generated at boot, and never emits a trigger_fired line. The whole purpose of the keeper is unwired in production.

The price-loop hardcodes 'use DEEP oracle for base and SUI oracle for quote' and quoteDecimals: 9 with comments 'Default SUI decimals; manifest-driven in production' and 'Full manifest-driven mapping is handled in the manifest module'. Neither is true: there is no manifest module, and runOnePollCycle IS the production path. A SUI/USDC pool would silently use the wrong quote decimals (USDC = 6) and the wrong oracle pair. This is the same coupling failure as R2-002 (no abstraction layer between vault.pool_id and oracle pair).

PollCycleArgs declares pollIntervalMs and deepCoinId as required fields. The function destructures them but never references them in the body (deepCoinId is only meaningful inside trigger submission — which doesn't happen, see R2-001; pollIntervalMs is the loop scheduler's concern, not a per-tick input). These dead args force every caller (including T-009 test) to pass placeholder values that mean nothing.

T-009 is genuine — the keeper's runOnePollCycle uses raw fetch JSON-RPC against manifest.network.rpcUrl and never imports any DeepBook helper SDK. The architectural commitment to 'no @mysten/deepbook-v3' is solid in package.json. However, because main() reuses the test seam unchanged (R2-001), a future maintainer who adds trigger submission to main() may import additional client surface (e.g. SuiJsonRpcClient) without re-running T-009 against the new main path. The lockdown locks down the test seam, not the production loop. This is the Cycle 1 lesson half-applied.

The trigger loop iterates registry.iterate() and (once R2-001 is fixed) would await signAndSubmitTrigger per vault. Because the main loop awaits runOnePollCycle and only then schedules the next tick, intra-tick double-fire is prevented by sequential iteration plus registry.markTriggered. However, there is no in-flight guard: if a tick takes longer than pollIntervalMs (e.g. RPC slowdown), Node's setTimeout will fire on schedule but await ordering serializes them — fine for correctness, but the contract permits parallel submission. If the implementer later adds Promise.all for parallelism, two ticks can race against the same vault before markTriggered lands. Worth flagging as a future-design hazard rather than a current bug.
impacts: AC3.10 (keeper builds AND submits the trigger transaction signed with the ephemeral key) is unsatisfied at runtime. AC3.12 keeper-side prerequisite (trigger_fired log line, owner-routed output) cannot be observed. This is exactly the Cycle 1 'structural fix that doesn't actually wire through' regression class the contract calls out under Implementation guidance. Tests pass because T-009 only asserts on the discovery+price half and the trigger evaluation produces logTriggerAttempt without further wiring.

title: parsePriceFromBcs accepts 34-byte exact match but does not warn on length-mismatch overshoot
recommendations: After parsePriceFromBcs, compare publishTimeSeconds to Date.now()/1000. Document the threshold in notes/pyth-shape.md (the file already says staleness is out of scope but the dimension prompt says detection is required).

Tighten the check to `bytes.length !== PRICE_BCS_LENGTH` and throw with a clear 'BCS layout drift detected: expected 34 bytes, got N — see notes/pyth-shape.md and re-capture' message. The G-Pyth escalation pathway then fires as designed.
descriptions: parsePriceFromBcs returns publishTimeSeconds, and notes/pyth-shape.md per the contract documents it as 'parsed but not enforced'. A paused feed returning the same price for 10 minutes would still be passed through to execute_trigger, which would fire on stale data.

The check is `if (bytes.length < PRICE_BCS_LENGTH) throw`. If devInspect returns 35+ bytes (e.g., upstream Pyth bumps the Price struct, adding a new field — exactly the G-Pyth escalation trigger), the decoder reads the first 34 bytes silently and ignores the rest. Owner gets executed at a price the market has since moved away from. This is the exploit class the dimension prompt explicitly flagged ('what if Pyth feed is stale or paused? Keeper should detect').

If the bundled Pyth package is upgraded mid-cycle and the Price struct grows a field, the keeper silently mis-decodes and either reads wrong values or reads correct values but misses new defense-relevant fields (e.g., a status flag indicating the feed is paused).

Implementation immediately calls process.exit(0) inside the signal handler. There is no await on any in-flight promise; the running flag is set to false but never checked between exit and the next loop iteration; an in-progress signAndSubmitTrigger (once R3-001 is fixed) would be killed mid-flight. Additionally, both handlers can fire reentrantly (no idempotency guard).

Contract Behavior > Lifecycle says the keeper installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that "stop the two loops, drain in-flight transactions, log a `keeper_shutdown` line, and exit zero". The implementation logs the line and immediately calls process.exit(0) inside the handler, with no await on any in-flight `signAndSubmitTrigger` (in fairness, no submission is wired in at all — see R6-008 — but the lifecycle behavior is still wrong). If a trigger is mid-submission when the signal lands, the in-flight HTTP request to sui_executeTransactionBlock continues on the Sui side and the tx may land on-chain after the keeper has already logged shutdown.

title: Pyth BCS Option<u64> parse for tp_price/sl_price misses the {None: true} encoding
recommendations: Run an actual create_vault against the live sandbox, capture the suix_queryEvents response for the VaultCreated event, and pin the exact encoding observed in a fixture (analogous to notes/pyth-shape.md's BCS capture). The test currently uses an assumed shape, not a captured one.
descriptions: parseOptionU64 treats `null` and `undefined` as None, plus any object with `Some` as Some. Sui's parsedJson encoding for Move Option<u64> (per the suix_queryEvents JSON-RPC response format) sometimes appears as `null` (when the SDK normalizes None) and sometimes as the literal object `{ None: true }` depending on SDK version and event source. The current parser falls through the second branch and returns null only via the catch-all comment 'Treat any other falsy shape as None' — but `{ None: true }` is truthy and a non-null object, so it would actually MATCH the `'Some' in raw` check (no — it wouldn't, but it also wouldn't return null cleanly either; it falls through the second `if`). The comment claim is ambiguous; current branch returns null because `'Some' in {None:true}` is false, so the function returns null at the bottom. That's incidentally correct, but the test fixture only exercises `null` and `{ Some: '<n>' }`. If the running sandbox returns `{ None: true }` (which the SDK does emit for Move Options in some versions), behavior is correct by accident; if it returns the structural enum form `{ Some: 'x' }` for Some / `null` for None it's also fine. The fragility is unlogged.
impacts: Risk class is misclassified-vault-fields. If the Sui SDK on the live sandbox uses a tagged-union encoding the parser isn't tested against (e.g., `{ Some: { value: '12345' } }` or a plain string '12345' for u64), tp_price/sl_price end up null when they should not — which silently disables the TP/SL gate for that vault.

recommendations: Check resp.ok and gasPriceJson.error. On any failure throw a clear 'reference gas price unavailable' error so the upstream catch logs trigger_failed with an actionable abort_code_or_message. Do not fabricate a default gas price.
descriptions: Two issues in the gas-price fetch path: (1) gasPriceResp.ok is never checked. A 5xx from the RPC returns an HTML body that fails JSON.parse silently (or returns gasPriceJson.result undefined). (2) On undefined result, the keeper silently substitutes 1000n MIST as the gas price. If the network's reference gas price is higher, transactions get rejected with confusing 'gas price too low' errors that look like a Move abort rather than an RPC outage.
impacts: Trigger submissions fail with the wrong error message when the RPC is degraded; the abort_code_or_message logged in trigger_failed misleads the operator. The fabricated 1000n is also a magic number not tied to any documented localnet value.

title: Logger emitter signatures use type-erasing 'as unknown as Record' cast that defeats safety
recommendations: Either (a) destructure each emitter's known fields exactly as logKeeperStarted does and pass that explicit object to emit(), removing the cast; or (b) drop the per-event TypeScript interface and accept Record<string, unknown> + a runtime schema validator. Pick one direction and apply uniformly.

Either (a) remove logLevel from Config until a debug event surface lands, or (b) thread a logger factory createLogger(level: string) through the boot path that gates emit() against the configured level.
descriptions: Every emitter except logKeeperStarted forwards its args object via 'args as unknown as Record<string, unknown>'. The function emit() then iterates Object.entries and skips SECRET_KEYS — so secret-redaction does work for ad-hoc keys, but the type system stops giving any guarantee that the documented AC3.11 minimum field set is present. logKeeperStarted destructures explicitly (good); the others do not. This is a design inconsistency: either ALL emitters destructure to enforce field presence at the boundary, or all emitters accept an open record and rely on runtime defense alone.

config.ts parses KEEPER_LOG_LEVEL into Config.logLevel; the contract states it 'gates additional debug events'. logger.ts has no level-gating at all — every emit() unconditionally writes to stdout. There is no concept of debug events to gate. The config field is therefore inert state.
impacts: A future caller who mistakenly passes { vault_id, owner, pool_id, side } (no tp_price/sl_price) to logVaultDiscovered passes type-checking (the interface declares all fields required) but if a refactor relaxes the interface signature, the cast will silently swallow missing fields. Lower-impact than R2-001 through R2-006 because today's call sites are correct, but the pattern is fragile.

Operator expectation set by the config knob does not match runtime behavior. Either the knob should be removed, or debug-tier events should be added and gated behind it. As-is, an operator setting KEEPER_LOG_LEVEL=warn will still receive every info-level event.

title: Logger secret redaction shallow — does not recurse into nested objects or arrays
recommendations: Make redaction recursive: a serializer that walks objects and arrays, omitting any key in SECRET_KEYS at any depth. Or simpler — implement a JSON.stringify replacer that drops secret keys at every depth.
descriptions: buildLine iterates Object.entries(extra) at the top level only and skips keys in SECRET_KEYS. If a caller passes `{ keeper: { secretKey: '...' } }` or `{ keypairs: [{ privateKey: '...' }] }`, the redaction does not apply — the nested secret is serialized to stdout. Spec says 'never logged in full' for the ephemeral keypair, and the Logger T-007 test only validates top-level redaction, leaving the nested case untested.
impacts: Defense-in-depth gap. If a future patch passes a richer 'response' or 'context' object that happens to contain a privateKey field (e.g., serializing a full keypair object for debug), the secret leaks to stdout. The keeper key is ephemeral so the blast radius is small on localnet, but the rule exists for a reason and the implementation does not honor it.

title: T-006 amendment changed the test input to match a comment — the comment was right, but no test pins the SDK's u64 LE encoding for the original 32_404_071 value
recommendations: When R5-002 is fixed and runOnePollCycle calls buildTriggerTransaction, add an assertion that the resulting PTB's pure.u64 arg for current_price equals exactly the value calculateBaseQuotePrice produced. Alternatively, in T-006, parameterize the input by computing it from a calculateBaseQuotePrice fixture call so the two tests share the same arithmetic.

Add a vitest unit test for signAndSubmitTrigger with a fetch spy that returns a canned sui_executeTransactionBlock response containing a TriggerFired event with known field values; assert the returned TriggerFiredEventPayload has each field extracted correctly. This also gives R5-001's 'second test for signAndSubmitTrigger' a natural home.
descriptions: Per synthesis-notes.md, T-006's input value was amended from 32_404_071 (the value priceModel computes from the DEEP/SUI live capture in T-005) to 32_414_055 because the asserted bytes on line 89 are 0x67 0x99 0xee 0x01 = 0x01EE9967 = 32_414_055 (verified). The test is still meaningful — it pins that tx.pure.u64(N) emits 8-byte LE for some value of N. However, the input no longer corresponds to ANY priceModel output the rest of the suite computes; the chain of evidence 'Pyth bytes → priceModel → triggerSubmitter PTB' is broken. T-005 pins priceModel for the DEEP/SUI live shape to 7_142_857n, T-006 pins triggerSubmitter for 32_414_055n — those are unrelated numbers, and no test verifies that priceModel's output (whatever it actually is in production) is correctly forwarded into the PTB by the calling code. (Indeed, runOnePollCycle never calls triggerSubmitter at all per R5-002, so there is no production caller to test against.)

AC3.12 step 7 (contract.md lines 743-766) is called out as a 'keeper-side prerequisite for the spec's output coin routed to the owner obligation'. The verification path: read the trigger transaction's owned-objects diff via sui_getTransactionBlock and confirm Coin<Quote>, Coin<Base> residual, Coin<DEEP> residual all owned by vault.owner (NOT the keeper's address). The keeper's TriggerFired event-extraction code in signAndSubmitTrigger (lines 165-181) reads the event payload but does NOT read or verify ownership of the residual coins. No test asserts the keeper extracts the right field set from TriggerFired (the test that does test logTriggerFired in T-007 just verifies the logger writes its inputs — it does not verify those inputs are correctly extracted from the on-chain event). This is the classic 'pure-function tested, integration with on-chain shape untested' gap the contract calls out.
impacts: The test still catches a u64 LE serialization regression for the literal 32_414_055, but the 'price flowing end-to-end through the keeper' guarantee that the suite appears to provide is illusory. A bug that swapped the currentPrice argument with deepPerTrigger in buildTriggerTransaction's call site (no such call site exists today, but the moment R5-002 is fixed, one will) would not be caught.

Medium — without an end-to-end test that drives signAndSubmitTrigger against a recorded sui_executeTransactionBlock response and asserts the extracted TriggerFired payload field-by-field, AC3.12 step 7 cannot be claimed by this cycle's test suite. It is technically deferrable to manual operator verification (the contract's wording allows that for the live-sandbox half), but the 'keeper extracts the event correctly' half is unit-testable today and isn't tested.

title: Two competing parsing paths: SandboxManifest.pools typed as Record but contract uses array
recommendations: Read ~/workspace/deepbook-sandbox/sandbox/deployments/localnet.json shape during the design pass and pin SandboxManifest.pools to whatever the live sandbox emits. Add a JSON fixture under tests/fixtures/ captured from the live sandbox so the type and the runtime stay in sync.
descriptions: Contract Behavior step 1 references 'pools[]' (an array indexed by integer position) used to map vault pool_id to coin types. SandboxManifest in index.ts types pools as 'Record<string, { ... }>' (keyed by pool name). The networkShape test fixture uses { DEEP_SUI: { ... } }. Either is workable, but the type drift between contract wording and code, combined with the absence of any pool-resolution function (R2-002, R2-003, R2-004), makes the field shape untestable end-to-end. Whichever shape the live sandbox manifest uses is not captured anywhere in code.
impacts: When the manifest module lands (R2-004) the type may need to change, breaking the existing test fixture. Worth picking a canonical shape now and asserting against the live localnet.json.

title: Boot-time errors crash with unstructured console.error — no keeper_failed_to_start event
recommendations: Add a 'keeper_failed_to_start' error event to logger.ts and emit it before exiting. Include { error } so the consumer can render the cause. Keep exit code 1.
descriptions: If loadConfig throws on bad env, or fs.readFileSync throws on missing manifest, or Ed25519Keypair construction throws, the catch at the bottom of the file does console.error('Fatal error:', err) and process.exit(1). The structured-log consumer (Cycle 5 UI / E-007 harness) cannot distinguish 'keeper crashed at boot' from 'keeper never started' because no log line is emitted to stdout. AC3.11 enumerates keeper_started and keeper_shutdown but no boot-failure event.
impacts: Diagnosability gap. Cycle 5's UI cannot present a 'keeper failed to boot — check env' message because it has no structured signal. Operators must SSH and look at stderr to see the actual config error.

title: manifest interface duplicates SandboxManifest types that should live in a manifest module
recommendations: Drop deepCoinId and pollIntervalMs from PollCycleArgs unless / until trigger submission is wired in. If kept, mark them at least as 'unused-pending-AC3.10-wiring'.

Move SandboxManifest to a new src/manifest.ts (typed loadManifest(path) plus resolvePoolForVault). Keep index.ts focused on boot + lifecycle. Net: same LOC overall, better separation, the SUI/USDC pool gets handled correctly.
descriptions: PollCycleArgs declares deepCoinId and pollIntervalMs as required fields. The destructure at line 87 binds deepCoinId, but it is never referenced afterward; pollIntervalMs is never destructured at all. They appear in the type signature only because runOnePollCycle was supposed to call signAndSubmitTrigger (which needs deepCoinId). With trigger submission dead-coded (R4-001), these knobs are pure noise — every caller has to thread two arguments that have no effect.

SandboxManifest, the four package fields, the pyth oracle pair, and the pools record are inline-declared in index.ts and re-derived ad hoc in runOnePollCycle (manifest.packages.pyth?.packageId ?? '', manifest.pythOracles.deepPriceInfoObjectId, etc.). Compounds R4-010 — the contract suggested src/manifest.ts to own this type plus the pool resolution. As-is, the manifest type is the second-largest type in the codebase and it lives in the file with the longest function. Splitting it out (mirroring the contract's suggestion) makes index.ts ~30 LOC shorter and gives the SUI/USDC pool resolution a home.
impacts: Misleads readers and tests about what the function does. The T-009 test must construct fake values for fields that affect nothing.

index.ts is 359 LOC — the largest module in the keeper. Most of the bloat is two concerns living together: the entry point AND the manifest schema AND the discovery helper AND runOnePollCycle. Decomposition would cleanly halve it.

title: shutdown handler sets `running = false` but immediately process.exit — flag is dead code
recommendations: Drop the `running` flag and the while-loop guard, OR drop process.exit and let the loop see running=false at the next setTimeout resolve. Pick one shape; do not claim both.
Delete the `const rpcUrl = manifest.network.rpcUrl` line and the corresponding `void rpcUrl;` line. Net: -2 LOC, +1 unit of clarity.
Either use `import.meta.main` (Node ≥20.11) for the simplest 1-line check, or split main() into a separate `src/main.ts` entry point that just does `await main()` unconditionally. Drops 13 LOC.
descriptions: The shutdown handler does `running = false; logKeeperShutdown(...); process.exit(0);`. Because process.exit is synchronous and terminates the process before the next iteration of the while loop, the `running` boolean is never observed. The contract specified 'drain in-flight transactions' before exit — calling process.exit immediately defeats that. Either the boolean should actually gate the loop (drop process.exit, let the loop notice running=false at the next iteration boundary, then exit) or the boolean should be removed and the handler should just exit. As written, the pattern signals 'graceful shutdown' but provides none.

main() reads `const rpcUrl = manifest.network.rpcUrl;` on line 301 and is never used; line 343 has `void rpcUrl; // suppress unused warning — used by runOnePollCycle via manifest`. The comment is a confession that the variable is dead. The fix is trivial — remove the binding entirely.

The 5-line isMain check builds an ad-hoc URL-vs-argv comparison: `import.meta.url.endsWith(process.argv[1].replace(/\\/g, '/'))`. The standard Node/ESM idiom is `import.meta.main` (Node 20.11+) or `pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href === import.meta.url` from `node:url`. The current form silently breaks on Windows symlinks and on argv[1] containing query strings.
impacts: Misleading code that implies a graceful-drain pattern that does not exist; an in-flight trigger submission (once wired per R4-001) would be killed mid-transaction.
One dead local + one comment that exists only to silence the compiler. Two-line subtraction.

Bug-class smell on Windows; the regex `/\\/g` partially anticipates this but doesn't cover all edge cases. More importantly: this logic is in the wrong file. A 3-line `bin/keeper.js` shim that imports and calls main() would remove the entire isMain block.

Either the filter should be MoveEventType (more precise per the contract) or the synthesis-notes should be corrected.
impacts: Documentation/code mismatch propagates incorrect knowledge into FEEDBACK / RUNBOOK; no runtime defect today.

title: Vault registry preserves triggered flag across addOrUpdate but cannot recover from re-discovery without re-seed
recommendations: After addOrUpdate(... wasNew=true), call `await registry.seedTriggeredFromChain(vault.vault_id, getObject)` before logging vault_discovered (or as part of the discovery tick). The seed function exists; it's just never invoked.
descriptions: addOrUpdate preserves the existing triggered flag when the vault is already known. Good. But on a fresh keeper start, parseVaultCreatedEvent sets triggered=false unconditionally (vaultRegistry.ts:106), and the contract's 'Vault triggered ground-truth on restart' decision (#3) requires seedTriggeredFromChain to be called for each known vault before the trigger loop runs. The discoverVaultsTick at index.ts:266-282 calls addOrUpdate but never calls seedTriggeredFromChain. main()'s boot path (index.ts:293-344) also does not call it — there's no per-vault seed step before the loop. Result: a keeper restart immediately after a fire enters a doomed retry loop until the on-chain abort lands.
impacts: On restart-after-fire, the keeper will issue a doomed execute_trigger that aborts with EVaultTriggered=1002. The keeper logs trigger_failed (which is at least visible) and continues; the next poll repeats the doomed call. AC3.10 gas-waste, but no protocol-level damage.

title: VaultCreatedEventEnvelope has 8 fields, 7 of which are never read by the parser
recommendations: Either change the parser signature to accept just `{ parsedJson: Record<string, unknown> }` (and drop the rest of the envelope type) or actually use the envelope fields for things like dedup-by-eventSeq.
descriptions: VaultCreatedEventEnvelope declares { id, packageId, transactionModule, sender, type, parsedJson, bcs, timestampMs } but parseVaultCreatedEvent only reads `envelope.parsedJson`. The other seven fields exist purely to make discoverVaultsTick (in index.ts) build a complete envelope object that is then thrown away. This pushes complexity into the call site (index.ts lines 254-264 build the 8-field object from the raw RPC response) for zero benefit.
impacts: ~30 LOC across two files exist to construct and type fields nobody reads. Any new RPC field requires updating the type even though parser doesn't care.

title: BCS decoder hand-rolls u64 LE reads instead of using @mysten/sui/bcs
recommendations: Replace readU64LE + the manual offsets with `bcs.struct(...)` from @mysten/sui/bcs and call `.parse(bytes)`. The negative-price abort can wrap the parse result. notes/pyth-shape.md remains the canonical reference, but the code mirrors the layout declaratively.
descriptions: parsePriceFromBcs hand-implements readU64LE in a 6-line loop and indexes 5 manual offsets (0, 1, 9, 17, 18, 26). The file already imports `bcs` from '@mysten/sui/bcs' (used in buildGetPriceUnsafeTxKindB64). A simpler form would be a single bcs.struct({ priceNegative: bcs.bool(), priceMagnitude: bcs.u64(), conf: bcs.u64(), expoNegative: bcs.bool(), expoMagnitude: bcs.u64(), timestamp: bcs.u64() }).parse(bytes) — one declaration, no hand-counted offsets, decoder errors on length mismatch automatically. The contract explicitly references the SDK 2.x bcs API as preferred.
impacts: Off-by-one risk in offsets if the layout ever changes; ~25 LOC of hand-rolled bit-shifting that the SDK already provides; future maintainer must re-derive the layout from bytes vs. reading the schema.

title: logger has 8 typed emitters that all delegate to one untyped emit — collapse
recommendations: Replace the 8 emitters with one `log<E extends keyof EventMap>(level, event: E, fields: EventMap[E])`. Keep the SECRET_KEYS filter. Type safety improves and the file shrinks to ~40 LOC.
descriptions: Six of the eight emitter functions (logVaultDiscovered, logPollCycle, logTriggerAttempt, logTriggerFired, logTriggerFailed, logPythReadFailed, logKeeperShutdown) are identical one-liners that call emit('info'|'warn', '<event_name>', args as unknown as Record<string, unknown>). The 'as unknown as Record<string, unknown>' cast appears 7 times — that is exactly the smell that says the type wrapper is buying nothing. Only logKeeperStarted does anything non-trivial (it destructures to drop unknown fields, which is also redundant with the SECRET_KEYS filter inside emit). 60+ LOC could collapse to a single typed `log(level, event, fields)` plus per-event TypeScript types declared near the call sites.
impacts: Bloat: ~60 LOC for what one generic function does. Every new event name requires a new emitter, a new type, and a new test, with no actual safety gain (the cast erases the type).
evidence: emit('info', 'vault_discovered', args as unknown as Record<string, unknown>);

title: Logger redaction list misses ed25519 SDK 2.x getter and PrivateKey export shapes
recommendations: Add `getSecretKey`, `secret`, `mnemonic`, `entropy` to the redaction set; recurse one level for object values so nested secret-shaped keys are also dropped; add a vitest case in logger.test.ts that constructs a synthetic keypair-shaped object and asserts no `suiprivkey1` substring leaks into stdout.
descriptions: SECRET_KEYS = new Set(['secretKey', 'privateKey', 'seed']) is the redaction allow-list. Sui SDK 2.x Ed25519Keypair exposes the secret via `getSecretKey()` (returns a `suiprivkey1...` bech32 string) and `export()` (returns `{ schema, privateKey }`). The redaction key for the bech32 export is the function name `getSecretKey`, not a field name, so it cannot be redacted by key-name match if a developer ever does `logger.info('debug', { keypair })` or spreads the keypair object. Additionally, the logger only inspects top-level keys — nested `{ wallet: { privateKey: '...' } }` would leak. The spec.md `never logged in full` rule treats the logger as a defense-in-depth layer; the Set is the entire defense.
impacts: Defense-in-depth weakening. The current code path doesn't pass the keypair to the logger anywhere (verified by grep), so this is dormant; but a future change that does so would silently leak the secret key. There is no test that asserts a keypair-shaped object cannot be logged.
evidence: const SECRET_KEYS = new Set(['secretKey', 'privateKey', 'seed']);

title: T-009 fetch spy returns identical canned BCS for DEEP and SUI Pyth reads — magnitude collision passes silently
recommendations: Inspect the request body for the priceInfoObjectId argument and return DEEP-shape bytes for the DEEP oracle ID, SUI-shape bytes for the SUI oracle ID. Then add an assertion that priceResults contains two distinct magnitudes (3_058_022n and 94_371_860n per the live captures in notes/pyth-shape.md). This costs ~10 lines and converts a tautology into a real check.
descriptions: The spy returns the same 34-byte BCS payload for every sui_devInspectTransactionBlock call regardless of which PriceInfoObject was requested. The green log confirms: poll_cycle line shows DEEP and SUI both with magnitude 3058022 and exponent -8 (DEEP price reused for SUI). The test is intentionally about 'outbound HTTP shape' so this works for its narrow purpose, but it means the test cannot detect a regression where the keeper accidentally passes the DEEP PriceInfoObject ID for both Pyth reads (and never reads SUI at all). The only line that distinguishes which oracle was read is the URL/body content, not the response.
impacts: Low — the test's stated purpose is HTTP-shape lockdown, not price-correctness. But anyone reading the green log might be misled into thinking the keeper successfully read both oracles distinctly, when in fact the canned data masks an entire class of pool-routing bugs.

title: T-001 missing-field tests do not cover normalize-hex path on uppercase / no-prefix input
recommendations: Add two cases: (a) tpslEvent({ vault_id: '0xABC123' + 'A'.repeat(58) }) and assert the parsed vault_id is the lowercase form; (b) tpslEvent({ owner: 'deadbeef' + 'b'.repeat(56) }) (no 0x prefix) and assert the parsed owner starts with '0x'. Three lines each.
descriptions: T-001's behavior text demands: 'vault_id and pool_id are normalized 0x-prefixed lowercase hex'. The fixtures pre-supply already-lowercase 0x-prefixed values (`'0xabc123' + 'a'.repeat(58)`) — so the normalizeHex code path that lowercases an uppercase address, or that prepends '0x' when the chain returns the bare hex, is never actually exercised. parseVaultCreatedEvent's call to normalizeHex on rawVaultId / rawOwner / rawPoolId could be entirely deleted (returning the raw string back) and the existing test would still pass; the lowercase + 0x-prefix assertions on lines 66-69 trivially hold for input that is already lowercase + 0x-prefixed. The 'side: 1 is preserved' test does pin the type-coerce, but the hex-normalize path is untested.
impacts: Low — Sui's parsedJson convention is to emit lowercase 0x-prefixed addresses anyway, so a regression that breaks the normalize path is unlikely to bite in production. But the test claims to verify the normalization and does not.

title: T-003 has no oversized-BCS fixture; trailing-bytes attacker payload silently parses as a valid price
recommendations: Either add a fixture with 50 bytes that asserts parsePriceFromBcs throws (tightening the guard to ===) or asserts it returns the leading-34-byte interpretation (documenting the lenient-parse behavior). Either is fine — the choice should be explicit, not accidental.
descriptions: T-003 covers a too-short (33 byte) input that throws, and the BCS-positive / negative / negative-price-abort cases. It does NOT cover the symmetric oversized case: a 50-byte input where the first 34 bytes are a valid price and the remaining 16 are garbage. parsePriceFromBcs's guard is `if (bytes.length < PRICE_BCS_LENGTH) throw` — strictly less-than, so a 50-byte input passes the guard and decodes the leading 34 bytes as a price, silently ignoring the trailing garbage. This is probably fine on the happy path (devInspect returns exactly 34 bytes), but a malformed Pyth response or a spec change to wrap the price in a different envelope would parse silently as the wrong thing.
impacts: Low — production Pyth devInspect returns exactly 34 bytes today. But the test promises a coverage envelope it does not actually deliver: 'truncated BCS' is covered, 'oversized BCS' (defense in depth) is not.

title: TP/SL precedence in evaluator matches Move correctly — confirmed against Move source
recommendations: No action required. Optionally add a one-line comment noting that the tie-break is purely a keeper-side log/diagnostic choice (not a Move-observable distinction).
descriptions: Reviewed the TP-then-SL ordering against the Move contract at tpsl_vault.move:147-149: `let tp_met = vault.tp_price.is_some() && current_price >= *vault.tp_price.borrow(); let sl_met = vault.sl_price.is_some() && current_price <= *vault.sl_price.borrow(); assert!(tp_met || sl_met, ETriggerConditionNotMet);`. The Move-side assertion only checks 'either gate met'; it does NOT actually distinguish which one fired. The keeper's evaluator returns 'tp' when both are met, which the test (T-004) pins. Since the Move contract emits a single TriggerFired event regardless and the swap path is the same either way, the keeper's tie-break is observationally indistinguishable from Move's behavior. No correctness bug — the keeper's choice of 'tp' is fine, and the assertion in the test is what 'matches Move' means here (Move evaluates `tp_met` first via short-circuit but does not preserve which one fired). Filed for clarity since the dispatch prompt asked specifically about this.
impacts: None — the precedence question has no observable user-facing consequence given the Move contract collapses both branches into a single event.

title: BCS sign-handling for price/expo correctly mirrors sandbox market-maker — verified
recommendations: No action required.
descriptions: Reviewed parsePriceFromBcs against the canonical sandbox reference at ~/workspace/deepbook-sandbox/sandbox/scripts/market-maker/price-feed.ts:28-41. The 34-byte layout (price.negative byte at offset 0, magnitude u64 LE at 1, conf u64 LE at 9, expo.negative byte at 17, expo.magnitude u64 LE at 18, timestamp u64 LE at 26) matches; the negative-price abort matches; the exponent reconstruction `expoNegative ? -expoMagnitude : expoMagnitude` matches. The notes/pyth-shape.md file documents real captured bytes (DEEP and SUI) and the parser correctly decodes them — the tests use the same captured magnitudes (3_058_022 and 94_371_860) and pass. Sign-bit handling is correct because Pyth's I64 BCS encoding is NOT two's-complement — it's a struct {negative: bool, magnitude: u64}, so the parser doesn't need bit manipulation. The dispatch's concern about 'sign-bit handling for two's-complement at the BCS layer' does not apply: the on-wire encoding sidesteps it entirely.
impacts: None — confirmed correct.
evidence: const exponent = expoNegative ? -expoMagnitude : expoMagnitude;

title: synthesis-notes Transaction#serialize() deprecation note — the keeper does not call serialize at all
recommendations: Migrate the T-006 test from tx.serialize() to tx.getData() per the SDK 2.0 docs. Production source needs no change.
descriptions: synthesis-notes flagged Transaction#serialize() deprecation. Searching the keeper source: serialize() is not called anywhere in src/ — only in the test file (tests/triggerSubmitter.test.ts uses it for structural inspection). So the deprecation does not affect production. The simplicity finding is on the test side: T-006 binds to `Transaction.serialize()` which the SDK has marked deprecated. title: Pyth-trust model is load-bearing and undocumented in keeper source
recommendations: Add a one-line module-comment at the top of triggerSubmitter.ts (and/or in notes/pyth-shape.md) stating: "The Move contract trusts the keeper-supplied current_price; the keeper is the price oracle from the contract's perspective.
